HEARD:
June 5, 2009

Herman J.

[
1
]

Mr. Alnoor Virani, as Estate Trustee for the Estate of Yasmin Peerwani,
seeks dismissal of Ms. Laljee’s action on the basis that it is statute-barred.

Section 38
of the
Trustee Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. T. 23 provides for a
limitation of two years after the death of a deceased.  Ms. Laljee’s action was
brought more than two years after the death of Ms. Peerwani.

[
2
]

Ms. Dee Dilshad Laljee puts forward two reasons why she did not
institute the claim within the two-year limitation period: she was ill; and Mr.
Virani led her to believe that she would be taken care of so that there was no
need for her to bring a claim.

Background

[
3
]

Ms. Laljee is the sister of the deceased, Yasmin Peerwani.  Mr. Virani
is Ms. Laljee’s uncle and the Estate Trustee of Ms. Peerwani’s estate.

[
4
]

Ms. Peerwani died on April 22, 2003.  Ms. Peerwani’s spouse brought
proceedings to contest the validity of the will.

[
5
]

Ms. Laljee is not a beneficiary under the will.   She did, however,
participate in the estate proceedings as estate trustee for the estate of her
father, Ismail Wadiwalla.  Mr. Wadiwalla was a beneficiary under the will and
died in August 2004.

[
6
]

According to Mr. Virani, a settlement of the estate proceedings was reached
on January 11, 2006.

[
7
]

By letter dated February 7, 2006, the solicitor for the estate of Mr.
Wadiwalla advised that he was no longer representing the estate.  Ms. Laljee did
not retain new counsel.

[
8
]

On March 3, 2006, Ms. Laljee advised that she would not sign the minutes
of settlement.  As a result, Ms. Peerwani’s spouse brought a motion.

[
9
]

On November 15, 2006, at the hearing of the motion, Ms. Laljee stated
that she intended to bring a claim against the estate for financial
compensation for the care that she had provided to Ms. Peerwani.  Justice
Klowak ordered the parties in the estate litigation to attend mediation.  She
also ordered that Ms. Laljee issue any claim on or by December 7, 2006, without
prejudice to any of the parties raising the defence that the claim was
statute-barred.

[
10
]

A
mediation was held in November 2007 but did not result in a settlement.

[
11
]

Ms. Laljee initiated her claim on December 1, 2006, more than three and
a half years after the death of Ms. Peerwani.

Ms. Laljee’s Claim

[
12
]

Ms.
Laljee’s claims arise from services that she says she provided to her sister
during her sister’s lifetime, caring for her sister and looking after the
household while her sister was ill.  She says that her sister told her that she
would be properly compensated and receive a substantial benefit from the estate
for all her work.  The plaintiff claims that, in reliance on her sister’s
promises, she made professional and personal sacrifices and expended years’
worth of work to her detriment.

[
13
]

Ms.
Laljee seeks $750,000 or a lesser amount equal to the value of her sister’s
estate.  She sets forward alternative claims on the basis of: constructive
trust and unjust enrichment; proprietary estoppel;
quantum meruit
; and
breach of contract.

Does the limitation in the
Trustee Act
apply
to Ms. Laljee’s claim?

[
14
]

Subections
38(2) and (3) of the
Trustee Act

provide:

(2) Except in cases of libel and slander, if a
deceased person committed or is by law liable for a wrong to another in respect
of his or her person or to another person’s property, the person wronged may
maintain an action against the executor or administrator of the person who
committed or is by law liable for the wrong.

(3) An action under this section shall not be brought
after the expiration of two years from the death of the deceased.

[
15
]

The
first issue is whether Ms. Laljee’s claim fits under this section, that is
whether it is “a wrong to another in respect of his or her person or to another
person’s property”.

[
16
]

In
the case of
Smallman v. Moore
,
1948 CanLII 4 (SCC)
, [1948] S.C.R. 295, the Supreme Court
considered the meaning of the words “wrong to another in respect of his
person”.  In that case, the plaintiff brought an action against the deceased’s
estate for breach of promise to marry.   Locke J. stated that it was the nature
of the injury rather than the form of the action which had to be determined.
He concluded that the wrong in this case constituted “a wrong to another in
respect of his person”.

[
17
]

The
Ontario Court of Appeal applied the
Smallman

case in
Roth v. Weston
Estate
,
1997 CanLII 1125 (ON CA)
, 36 O.R. (3d) 513 (C.A.) to conclude that the alleged conduct fell
within s. 38 (2), noting that the plaintiff’s case was “focused on the personal
conduct of the deceased, the personal duty alleged to be owing by the deceased
to the plaintiff, and the resulting personal consequence to the plaintiff”.

[
18
]

The
plaintiff’s claim in
Ethier v. Raspberry
,
[1997] O.J. No. 666 (Gen.
Div.)
; aff’d
1998 CarswellOnt4483 (Div. Ct.)
is similar to Ms. Laljee’s.

The
plaintiff claimed that for a period of twenty years, she took care of the
deceased who, in return for these services, promised the plaintiff that she
would be paid by the estate.  However, the deceased did not leave her anything
in the will.  The plaintiff claimed breach of contract,
quantum meruit
fraudulent
misrepresentation, unjust enrichment and constructive trust. On an appeal to
the Divisional Court, Southey J. stated that, as in the
Roth
case, the
plaintiff’s claim was focused on the personal conduct of the deceased, the personal
duty alleged to be owed by the deceased to the plaintiff and the resulting
personal consequences to the plaintiff.  He concluded that all of the claims
were statute-barred by
s. 38 (3)
of the
Trustee Act
.

[
19
]

I
conclude that the essence of Ms. Laljee’s claim is a claim of a personal
nature, focusing on the conduct of the deceased, the personal duty that she
says the deceased owed to her and the resulting personal consequences.  It
therefore constitutes a “wrong to another in respect of his or her person”,
within the meaning of
s. 38 (2)
of the
Trustee Act
.

Does the
Limitations
Act
apply?

[
20
]

Ms. Peerwani died on April 22, 2003, at a time when the former
Limitations
Act
,
R.S.O. 1990, c. L.15
was in force.  Under the former Act, the
applicable limitation period was six years.

[
21
]

The
Court of Appeal considered a similar situation in
Smith Estate v. College of
Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario
,
1998 CanLII 1523 (ON CA)
, [1998] O.J. No. 4367 (C.A.).  When Dr.
Smith’s cause of action arose, the applicable limitation period was six years.
However, Charron J. concluded that as a result of Dr. Smith’s death, the
limitation period was reduced to two years from his death.

[
22
]

Similarly,
in
English Estate v. Tregal Holdings Ltd.
,
[2004] O.J. No. 2853 (Sup.
Ct.)
, Pepall J. noted that the provisions of
s. 38
of the
Trustee Act

were not altered by the new
Limitations Act
, 2002 S.O. 200, c. 24,
although she concluded that the claim in that case was not for injury of a
personal nature and was therefore not captured by s. 38.

[
23
]

The
issue was also considered by Lederer J. in
Kramarz v. KMH Cardiology &
Diagnostic Centres
(2007), 87 O.R. (3d) (Sup. Ct.).  He considered the
transition provisions in the new
Limitations Act
, 2002 and concluded
that because the limitation in the
Trustee Act
existed before the new
Limitations
Act
, the transition provisions did not apply.

[
24
]

I therefore conclude that the two-year limitation period in the
Trustee
Act
applies.

Does the court
have any discretion to extend the limitation period?

[
25
]

Ms.
Laljee submits that the limitation period should be extended given the circumstances.
She puts forward two reasons for failing to bring her claim within the two-year
limitation period: she was ill during the period; and her uncle, Mr. Virani,
the Estate Trustee led her to believe that she would be taken care of under the
estate.

[
26
]

Mr.
Virani maintains that Ms. Laljee was well aware of the situation and would have
been able to bring her claim within the two-year limitation period.

[
27
]

Does the court have any discretion to extend the
Trustees Act

limitation period?

[
28
]

In
Waschkowski
v. Hopkinson Estate
(2000),
2000 CanLII 5646 (ON CA)
, 47 O.R. (3d) 370 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal
considered whether the discoverability rule could extend the limitation period
in
s. 38
where the injured person did not discover that there was a basis for
an action until after the two years had expired.  Based on the language of the
provision, Abella J.A. concluded that the discoverability rule did not apply.
The only applicable limitation period was the two-year period in
s. 38
.  She
articulated the underlying policy considerations of having a clear time limit
as follows (at para. 9):

The draconian legal impact of the common law was that
death terminated any possible redress for negligent conduct.  On the other
hand, there was a benefit to disposing of estate matters with finality.  The
legislative compromise in
s. 38
of the
Trustee Act

was to open a
two-year window, making access to a remedy available for a limited time without
creating indefinite fiscal vulnerability for an estate.

[
29
]

Rosenberg,
J.A. noted in
Bikur Cholim Jewish Volunteer Services v. Langston
,
2009 ONCA 196 (CanLII)
, [2009]
O.J. No. 841 (C.A.) at para
33
, that the harshness of the conclusion in
Waschkowski

was somewhat mitigated by the application of the doctrine of fraudulent concealment.

[
30
]

The
doctrine of fraudulent concealment was considered in the case of
Giroux
Estate v. Trillium Health Centre
,
2004 CanLII 18056 (ON SC)
, [2004] O.J. No. 557 (Sup. Ct.).  In that
case, Lederman J. held that the doctrine of fraudulent concealment could be
used to a postpone limitation period.  He summarized the law of fraudulent
concealment, indicating at para. 20 that it applies where:

(a) the defendant and
plaintiff are engaged in a special relationship with another;

(b) given the special or
confidential nature of their relationship, the defendant’s conduct amounts to
an unconscionable thing for the one to do towards the other;

(c) the defendant conceals the plaintiff’s right of action (either
actively, or as a result of the manner in which the act that gave rise to the
right of action is performed).

[
31
]

The
decision was upheld on appeal
2005 CanLII 1488 (ON CA)
, [2005] O.J. No. 226 (C.A.).   Moldaver J.A.
contrasted the doctrine of fraudulent concealment to the discoverability rule,
noting at para. 28 that unlike the discoverability rule, the doctrine of
fraudulent concealment is not a rule of construction.  Rather it is an
equitable principle aimed at preventing a limitation period from operating “as
an instrument of injustice”.  Where it applies, it suspends the running of the
limitation clock until the injured party can reasonably discover the cause of
action.   The doctrine is aimed at preventing unscrupulous defendants who stand
in a special relationship with the injured party from using the limitation
provision as an instrument of fraud.

[
32
]

Ms.
Laljee claims that she did not institute an action sooner because her uncle,
Mr. Virani, the estate trustee, misled her into believing that she would be
looked after. She says that it was not until December 2005 that she fully
realized that her uncle had no intention of honouring his commitment that she
would be compensated.

[
33
]

In
her affidavit, Ms. Laljee refers to a conversation in June 2004 when her uncle
told her that she would be compensated for the years that she looked after her
sister and her sister’s children.   She says that her father assured her before
he died in August 2004 that her uncle had told him that she would be
compensated.  She claims that her uncle told her not to waste money on lawyers
making a claim because she would be compensated.  She also claims that a copy
of the will was withheld from her father for three years.

[
34
]

In
his affidavit, Mr. Virani says that Ms. Laljee was aware of the contents of the
testator’s will “at all relevant times” and had ample opportunity to bring the
claim within the two-year limitation period.

[
35
]

I
cannot, on the basis of the evidence before me, determine whether the doctrine
of fraudulent concealment would apply in this case: whether Ms. Laljee and Mr.
Virani have a special relationship; whether, given that relationship, Mr.
Virani’s conduct was unconscionable; and whether Mr. Virani concealed Ms.
Laljee’s right of action either by assuring her that she would be compensated
for or by withholding a copy of the will.

[
36
]

In
the result, I am unable to determine whether Ms. Laljee’s action is
statute-barred.  It is a triable issue.  The motion is therefore dismissed.

[
37
]

It
is now more than six years since the deceased died.  According to Mr. Virani,
there are insufficient funds in the estate to fully satisfy all the bequests.  Neither
the Estate nor Ms. Laljee stands to benefit from costly litigation.  I have
considered whether the issue of the limitation period should be referred to a
trial of the issue but I am concerned that the result of doing so would add to
the costs and result in further delay.  It would be to the benefit of both
parties to either resolve the dispute or proceed to trial expeditiously.

[
38
]

As
far as I can determine, Ms. Laljee has not yet filed a reply to the statement
of defence.  If that is the case, she has 15 days within which to do so.

[
39
]

The
parties have not yet had an opportunity to make submissions on costs.  My inclination
would be to reserve costs to the trial judge since I have not determined the
limitation period issue.  If either party disagrees with this, they may provide
brief written submissions (no more than 3 pages in length) within 7 days.  The
other party has a further 7 days within which to respond.  If I do not receive
any submissions, I will reserve costs to the trial judge.

___________________________

Herman J.
